top_choice_rationale: P001 (Autor, Hanson, Katz) answers a first-order question about who gains and loses when technology and trade shift labour demand. It pairs a skill-demand and supply framework with transparent local-labour-market designs that the field has re-examined for a decade or more. Reanalysis has refined magnitudes and persistence but has not overturned the robust findings: slow adjustment, geographic concentration of costs and weak reallocation. The citation should rest on those findings and on labour demand, wages and local labour markets, and should avoid effect-size claims and any claim of priority for the task model. Attribution is the main weakness, because Dorn is excluded and the technology and trade strands could be read as two achievements. I judge that a single coherent citation can be written. I rank P002 (Kiyotaki and Moore) second because its originator attribution is cleaner and it is mature, but its quantitative importance is established only indirectly and it overlaps partly with the 2022 prize. I rank no award last because both proposals are mature, substantive and citable.
recusal_note: none apparent from profile; my co-authors and ties (Camerer, Pfeiffer, Holzmeister, Huber, Nosek, Rand, Fudenberg, Nowak, Ellingsen, Johannesson, Brodeur) are not credited on any proposal. My metascience emphasis on replication and transparent identification is a perspective, not a connection.
